phonemes.desc: Voiced velar stop [g] plus long eta [ɛː]. The name is a single long syllable, the earth named as one continuous thing.

pronunciation.approximation: 'GAY' — one long, level syllable, like the sustained note of a deep drum.

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: Γῆ (Gê/Gē), the earth as goddess and as solid ground

kin.label: PIE
kin.form: *dʰéǵʰōm, 'earth'; Greek γῆ and Latin humus are related derivatives

kin.label: Homeric
kin.form: Γαῖα (Gaîa), the more metrical and later poetic form of the name

pronunciation.note: Gē is Tier 1 because the Greek Γῆ bears the circumflex, which marks both stress and the long vowel (eta) in a single accent — both features the ASCII form loses. It is the older cultic form of the earth goddess, later often called Gaîa in poetry.

domains.title: The Earth Itself
domains.subtitle: Motherhood, Fertility, Primordial Ground
domains.lead: Gē is the earth as goddess, the primordial ground from which gods, Titans, and mortals arise. She is not a distant creator but the very substance beneath our feet, venerated in every Greek city and invoked in oaths, harvests, and burials.

cards.name: Mother of All
cards.desc: From Gē spring the Titans, the Giants, the Erinyes, and — with Ouranos — the whole cosmos.

cards.name: Giver of Crops
cards.desc: Agricultural fertility and the annual return of grain depend on her body.

cards.name: Tomb and Womb
cards.desc: She receives the dead and regenerates life; grave and cradle are the same soil.

cards.name: Oracle of the Dead
cards.desc: Her chthonic power underlies oracles and dream-visions at sanctuaries of the underworld.

symbols.name: Cornucopia
symbols.meaning: The abundance that rises from her soil

symbols.name: Serpent
symbols.meaning: The earth-bound creature that glides through her body and guards her sanctuaries

symbols.name: Oak or olive tree
symbols.meaning: The rooted life that grows directly from her

symbols.name: Black stone
symbols.meaning: Aniconic representation of the earth goddess at numerous archaic shrines

mythology.lead: Gē is a primordial power whose myths are acts of generation and revenge. She creates without a mate, then conspires with her son Kronos against her husband Ouranos — and when the Titans fall, she arms the gods' last enemy.

myths.title: Broad-Breasted, First of All
myths.text: First came Chaos; then Gē, 'broad-breasted,' the ever-sure seat of all the immortals who hold the peaks of snowy Olympus — and with her dark Tartaros in the depths, and Eros, fairest among the deathless gods (Hesiod, Theogony 116–122). Gē needs no consort for her first births: Ouranos, starry heaven, her equal in size, to cover her all around; the long Mountains, delightful haunts of the nymphs; and Pontos, the barren deep with its swelling breast (Theogony 126–132). The reverence behind the poem is far older than Hesiod — the Mycenaean tablets already know ma-ka, Mother Earth — and the goddess is present wherever Greeks stood on ground, every oath sworn 'by Earth' being hers. Before any god ruled, there was ground; before any temple, a floor of her body. The Theogony's opening makes one quiet claim that the whole poem then obeys: everything in it, Olympians included, will be a tenant of Gē.

myths.title: The Sickle of Adamant
myths.text: Gē grew weary of Ouranos, who night after night covered her and pushed the children she bore back into her womb, giving them no light (Hesiod, Theogony 156–160). She fashioned the great sickle of adamant and unburdened herself to her sons, but only Kronos, the youngest and most terrible, took the weapon and lay in ambush; when Ouranos came down covering her, Kronos reached out and struck — and the drops of blood that fell on Gē produced the Erinyes, the great Giants, and the ash-tree nymphs, while what fell into the white foam of the sea produced Aphrodítē (Theogony 173–200). Hesiod does not soften the scene: the mother arms the son against the father, and from that violence the next generation of powers is born. The cosmos changes hands not by negotiation but by surgery — and notice what Gē herself does with the power she wins. She does not seize the throne; she engineers the future and lets her children fight for it, remaining what she always was: the ground under every regime.

myths.title: Kourotrophos, Nurse of Children
myths.text: For all her cosmic acts, Gē's worship in the Greek cities was domestic and quiet. At Athens her altar stood in the Agora beside that of Gē Kourotrophos, Earth the Child-Nurse, among the crossroads shrines — modest stone and ash where marble would have been pretentious, and the excavated altars of the Agora still mark the spot. At Delphi the Pythia opened her formal prayer with Earth first — 'first in my prayer I honor Earth, the first prophetess' (Aeschylus, Eumenides 1–2) — because the oracular succession of the sanctuary began, in tradition, with Gē herself, before Themis, before Phoibe, before Apollo took the tripod. Oaths were sworn by her in court and treaty: she was the one power guaranteed to be standing under both parties' feet. The oldest goddess in Greece asks for almost nothing — which is exactly why she was never, anywhere, omitted.

myths.title: Typhon, Born in Anger
myths.text: When the Titans fell, Gē did not reconcile. Angry on her children's behalf, she lay with Tartaros in a hollow cave of Cilicia and bore her youngest and most terrible child: Typhoeus — a hundred serpent heads, fire for eyes, and voices that ranged from the language of gods to the bellowing of bulls (Hesiod, Theogony 820–835). The whole Olympian order trembled; Zeus met the monster with thunderbolt and sickle, burned its hundred heads, and cast it down wounded beneath the earth — and the flames that pour from Mount Aetna are, Hesiod says, the monster's breath to this day (Theogony 853–868). Apollodorus tells the parallel story of the Gigantomachy (Bibliotheca 1.6.3): Gē armed her Giant sons against the gods and hunted the magic herb that would make them unbeatable — Zeus got to it first, on Athena's advice. The mother who produced the gods also produces their last enemy. For Gē, creation and rebellion are the same act repeated — the ground brings forth whatever the age requires, against whoever currently rules.

lore.syncretism: Gē was identified early with the Minoan-Mycenaean earth mother and later with the Anatolian Cybele and the Roman Terra Mater. In Orphic cosmogonies she is sometimes preceded by Night or Water, but she remains the foundational maternal power. Neoplatonists interpreted her as the material substrate of the visible world, the 'receptacle' of becoming. Modern ecological movements have reclaimed Gaia/Gē as a symbol of the living planet.
lore.culturalLegacy: The name Gē survives in English 'geo-' (geology, geography, geometry) and in the scientific Gaia hypothesis, which proposes that Earth functions as a self-regulating system. She is the oldest layer of Greek religion: not a specialist deity but the ground of all being. Every seed planted and every body buried returns to her, making her the most democratic of goddesses.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Gē does not choose sides; she is the board on which the game is played. Titans and Olympians alike are her children, and in the end all bodies return to her. This gives her a strange neutrality: she can conspire against the sky and still receive the sky-god's thunderbolts into her breast.

To meditate on Gē is to remember dependence. We do not stand apart from nature; we stand on it. The modern ecological crisis is, at root, a forgetting of Gē — a pretense that the ground is merely resource rather than kin. Restoring her name in Unicode is a small symbolic act of remembering that the earth is older than all our conflicts and more patient than all our gods.
lore.archaeology: Gē was worshipped at numerous sites without always receiving monumental temples. The Athenian Agora preserves her altar and that of Gē Kourotrophos near the crossroads. Aniconic stones, pits for liquid offerings, and boundary markers attest her chthonic cult across Greece. The Pythion at Athens and the Eleusinion also honor her as the maternal earth underlying Demeter's mysteries.
